strengths: The paper makes a useful and original practical contribution by generating virtual correspondences from point coordinates and composing established 5-point/6-point and P3P solvers. The mean-based variants offer a particularly simple approach to difficult three-view configurations. Their demonstrated usefulness and low implementation burden support weak acceptance.

The calibrated experiments provide meaningful evidence across 10,000 image triplets. In Table 1, 4p3v(M±δ) improves AUC@10 over the homotopy-continuation baseline from 50.61 to 52.27 on Sacre Coeur and from 32.03 to 32.53 on St. Peter’s Square. These improvements accompany a substantially simpler method.

The evaluation includes valuable conventional baselines, oracle comparisons, noise and outlier experiments, and perturbation sensitivity studies. The manuscript explicitly acknowledges approximation error and reports that 5pt+P3P can outperform the proposed methods. This makes the comparison between sampling configurations informative beyond the proposed algorithms themselves.

Additional experiments demonstrate practical potential. On KITTI, the mean-based perturbed solver achieves AUC@5 of 72.05 versus 71.73 for 6pt+P3P, with reported runtime decreasing from 0.11 to 0.07 seconds. The supplementary two-view experiment also demonstrates a useful accuracy–runtime tradeoff: 0.02 versus 0.04 seconds, with AUC@5 decreasing from 63.71 to 61.80.
weaknesses: Validation does not cover all quantities required by the stated problems. The pose metric measures rotations and translation directions for pairs 1–2 and 1–3, but excludes their relative baseline scale. No focal-length estimation errors are reported either. Consequently, good scores do not establish accurate recovery of the complete three-camera configuration or the unknown focal length. The real 4p3vf evaluation is also restricted to KITTI stereo/adjacent-frame triplets, where limited relative rotation can make focal recovery poorly conditioned.

The claimed advantage under limited computational time is only partially established. Figure 3 compares RANSAC iteration counts, although the perturbed methods generate more hypotheses per iteration. Table 1 reports 218.71 microseconds per call for 4p3v(M±δ), versus 77.90 for 5pt+P3P, with learned variants costing substantially more. The outlier plots establish faster convergence in iterations; accuracy versus elapsed time is needed to substantiate the corresponding claim under a fixed time budget.

The reliability of the mean-point approximation remains incompletely characterized. Lemma 1 provides an epipolar-distance bound determined by triangle size, which can be large and does not bound pose error. Figure 6 confirms appreciable errors even with noiseless observations. Experiments varying perspective distortion, depth variation, and triangulation conditioning would clarify when the approximation produces useful hypotheses and when it fails. This limits the generality of the method, without negating its demonstrated empirical utility.

The learned component is less convincing than the mean-based contribution. For example, on Sacre Coeur, switching from M±δ to L±δ raises AUC@5 only from 44.51 to 44.89 while increasing solver time from 218.71 to 511.28 microseconds; improvements are not consistent across datasets and metrics. Additionally, Eq. (2) specifies a signed residual rather than a nonnegative Sampson loss. Minimizing that expression literally would not favor zero epipolar error. This may be a correctable formula error, but the actual training objective cannot be established from the manuscript.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful supplementary network details. RANSAC thresholds, stopping and local-optimization settings, and the KITTI sequence selection and triplet count are unspecified. Section 3.2 also leaves the learned solver’s coordinate normalization with unknown focal length and the joint perturbation of its two virtual correspondences unclear. Code release is promised, so it cannot presently resolve these omissions.
